wedge.question: Ingredient costs jumped. What should I change?
wedge.page_title: Cafe cost decision — three choices compared
wedge.headline: Ingredient costs are up {shock}%. What should you do?
wedge.hero_lede: Three ways to respond, compared on the same model of your cafe and the same assumptions. Only the decision changes between them.
wedge.what_changed: Your suppliers put ingredient prices up {shock}%.

world_verdict_labels.C: A 5% rise plus simplifying the menu

wedge.unknown_why: Everything here turns on how many customers you lose when the price goes up. Nobody knows that number for your cafe — the figure used comes from research on eating out as a whole.
wedge.unknown_how: Raise the price of a few items for two weeks and count the orders. Two weeks of your own till data beats any research figure we can offer.

sens_help.low: Loyal customers, or your competitors are raising prices too.
sens_help.central: The typical response found in research on eating out.
sens_help.high: Stress case: competitors hold their prices and customers have easy alternatives.

wedge.c_card_note: Depends on how much simplifying the menu cuts ingredient cost (about {red} points here) and how many {unit} leave with the removed items ({loss}%). Neither is measured from your cafe.
wedge.chart_lede: Costs take about a week to rise — you are still using stock bought at the old price. Customers take a couple of weeks to react to a new price.
wedge.sources_note: Research gives a reference range for eating out as a whole. Your own customers may be more or less price-sensitive than that.
limits_does_not: Know how your individual customers will behave.
Model the wider economy, seasons or new customers.

wedge.headline: هزینهٔ مواد اولیه {shock}٪ بالا رفته. چه کار کنی؟
wedge.hero_lede: سه راه واکنش، روی یک مدل از کافهٔ خودت و با همان فرض‌ها مقایسه شده‌اند. تنها چیزی که بینشان فرق می‌کند، خودِ تصمیم است.

world_verdict_labels.C: ۵٪ بالا بردن قیمت همراه با سبک‌کردن منو

wedge.uncertainty_title: مشتری‌های تو چقدر به قیمت حساس‌اند؟
wedge.unknown_why: همه‌چیز به این بستگی دارد که با بالا رفتن قیمت چند مشتری را از دست می‌دهی. این عدد برای کافهٔ تو معلوم نیست؛ عددی که استفاده شده از پژوهش دربارهٔ کل بیرون‌غذاخوردن می‌آید.

wedge.sources_note: پژوهش یک بازهٔ مرجع برای کل بیرون‌غذاخوردن می‌دهد. مشتری‌های خودت ممکن است حساس‌تر یا کم‌حساس‌تر باشند.

interventions.label: Raise average menu prices
interventions.description: Adds the given number of percentage points to the average menu price for the whole horizon. Magnitude is the price increase in percent.

interventions.label: Remove or reformulate low-margin items
interventions.description: Lowers average ingredient cost per order by the given number of percentage points of the pre-shock COGS, and costs a small share of orders from customers who came for the removed items. Magnitude is the COGS reduction in percentage points; the demand cost is a fixed ratio of it (expert assumption, see evidence registry).

event.label: Supplier prices +{shock}%
event.description: Ingredient / input prices rise and stay at the new level for 90 days.

options.label: Do nothing
options.headline: Hold prices. Absorb the full cost increase.

options.label: Raise prices 10%
options.headline: Pass most of the increase to customers with a 10% average price rise.

options.label: Raise prices 5% + trim the menu
options.headline: A smaller 5% price rise, plus removing or reformulating low-margin items to cut ingredient cost per order.

registry_spec.label: Share of orders on low-margin items
Price sensitivity of customers
registry_spec.assumption_source: No study supports this setting. andreyeva2010 backs the central value; bijmolt2005 is the upper reference the high setting was placed against.
registry_spec.note: A 1% price rise eventually reduces orders by this percentage. Low 0.50 / central 0.81 / high 1.60. This is the assumption most likely to change the decision.

registry_spec.label: Share of supplier increase reaching your costs
registry_spec.note: 100% by definition unless you can substitute, renegotiate or have fixed-price contracts (tested at 70%).

registry_spec.label: Delay before higher prices reach your costs
registry_spec.note: Fresh inventory turns over in roughly a week; costs then rise over a few more days.

registry_spec.label: How quickly customers react to a price change
Ingredient-cost saving from trimming the menu

value.text: {reduction:g} points off average ingredient cost ({reformulation_effectiveness:.2f} per point of low-margin share)

registry_spec.note: Tested at half and one-and-a-half times this rate.

registry_spec.label: Orders lost from removing items
registry_spec.note: One third of the ingredient-cost saving, in points of orders: customers who came for the removed items.

registry_spec.label: Price rises compared
registry_spec.note: The decisions being compared; fixed by the question.

registry_spec.label: Comparison horizon
registry_spec.note: Long enough for costs and most of the customer reaction to land; short enough that wages and rent can be treated as fixed. Slow customer reactions are not fully visible within it.

registry_spec.label: Average order value
registry_spec.note: Monthly sales divided by monthly orders.

sweep_labels.cogs_pass_through: How much of the supplier increase reaches your costs
sweep_labels.supplier_increase_pct: How large the supplier increase actually is
sweep_labels.reformulation_effectiveness: How much trimming the menu really saves

sources.citation: Andreyeva T, Long MW, Brownell KD. The impact of food prices on consumption: a systematic review of research on the price elasticity of demand for food. American Journal of Public Health. 2010;100(2):216-222. doi:10.2105/AJPH.2008.151415
sources.population: 160 US studies, 1938-2007; 13 estimates for the 'food away from home' category
sources.limitations: Category-level (primary demand): how much less the public eats out when eating out as a whole gets dearer. Not firm-level. US only. Studies up to 2007.
sources.transfer: Justified for the CENTRAL setting when the cost shock is market-wide and competitors also raise prices, so the cafe's price moves with the category. Not justified on its own for a single cafe raising prices while competitors hold theirs.

sources.citation: Bijmolt THA, van Heerde HJ, Pieters RGM. New empirical generalizations on the determinants of price elasticity. Journal of Marketing Research. 2005;42(2):141-156.
sources.population: 1,851 price elasticities from 81 studies, predominantly packaged consumer goods in retail scanner data
sources.limitations: Brand-level in supermarket categories with near-perfect substitutes on the same shelf. It measures switching between brands inside a shop, not switching between shops.
sources.transfer: Used as the upper reference point. For a shop it is the 'my customers can buy the identical thing elsewhere' end of the range; for a cafe it is further away still, and the HIGH setting of 1.60 there is a judgement placed between the food category CI top (1.07) and this mean.

intake_fields.label: Monthly sales
intake_fields.hint: Typical month, before the cost increase.

intake_fields.label: Monthly ingredient / input cost
intake_fields.hint: What you pay suppliers for what you sell. Not wages, not rent.

intake_fields.label: Monthly fixed costs
intake_fields.hint: Rent, wages, utilities, loan payments — everything that will not change in the next 90 days.

intake_fields.label: Cash available
intake_fields.hint: What is in the business account today.

intake_fields.label: Expected supplier cost increase
intake_fields.hint: The increase you are facing, as a percentage of your ingredient cost.

intake_fields.label: Share of orders on low-margin items
intake_fields.hint: Roughly what share of orders are items you could drop or reformulate. A guess is fine; it is tested as an assumption.
